statement: For every [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ and every $p \ge 0$, integration of [differential forms](c:differential-form) over smooth singular simplices induces an isomorphism $H^p_{dR}(M) \cong H^p(M; \mathbb{R})$ from [de Rham cohomology](c:de-rham-cohomology) to real [singular cohomology](c:singular-cohomology).

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) without boundary, Hausdorff and second countable.

conclusion: The de Rham map $[\omega] \mapsto (\sigma \mapsto \int_\sigma \omega)$ is an isomorphism $H^p_{dR}(M) \to H^p(M; \mathbb{R})$ for every $p \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Mayer-Vietoris induction over convex sets
proofs.slogan: Check the de Rham map on convex open sets, glue it along Mayer-Vietoris sequences, and spread it from charts to the whole manifold.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof for every smooth manifold, compact or not; steps 2, 4 and 5 rest on the cited chapter. For the empty manifold both sides are zero.

roles.why: Smoothness gives forms and smooth simplices; second countability gives the countable chart covers that the induction needs.

steps.slogan: Define the de Rham map by integration over smooth singular simplices.
steps.detail: Send a closed $p$-form $\omega$ to the [cochain](c:cochain) $\sigma \mapsto \int_\sigma \omega$ on smooth $p$-simplices. Stokes' theorem gives $\int_\sigma d\eta = \int_{\partial\sigma} \eta$, so the map commutes with the differentials and acts on cohomology.

steps.slogan: Identify smooth singular cohomology with ordinary singular cohomology.
steps.detail: Every continuous simplex is homotopic to a smooth one through smoothing operators that are chain homotopic to the identity. So the inclusion of smooth singular chains into all singular chains induces an isomorphism in cohomology.

steps.slogan: Prove the isomorphism for convex open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
steps.detail: On a convex open set the Poincaré lemma makes every closed $p$-form with $p \ge 1$ exact, and contractibility kills singular cohomology in positive degrees. In degree 0 both sides are the constants $\mathbb{R}$, and the map sends $1$ to $1$.

steps.slogan: Transfer the isomorphism from $U$, $V$ and $U \cap V$ to $U \cup V$.
steps.detail: The de Rham map commutes, up to sign, with the [Mayer-Vietoris sequences](c:mayer-vietoris-sequence) of both theories for the open cover $\{U, V\}$. The five lemma then makes the map for $U \cup V$ an isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Extend the isomorphism from convex sets to every open subset and then to $M$.
steps.detail: Induction with step 4 gives finite unions of convex sets, and disjoint unions follow because both theories turn them into products. A proper exhaustion function cuts $M$ into bands that are finite unions of convex chart sets; the even bands are disjoint, the odd bands too, so step 4 gives $M$.

concepts.c:smooth-manifold: The manifold carries the forms and the smooth simplices that are compared.
concepts.c:differential-form: Closed forms give the de Rham classes that are integrated.
concepts.c:de-rham-cohomology: It is the source of the map that the proof shows bijective.
concepts.c:singular-cohomology: It is the target, computed with smooth simplices after step 2.
concepts.c:cochain: Integration turns each closed form into a singular cochain.
concepts.c:mayer-vietoris-sequence: Both theories have it, which lets the isomorphism pass to unions.

source.ref: J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd edition, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 218, Springer, 2013, chapter 18 (The de Rham theorem)
source.note: Lee proves the theorem by this Mayer-Vietoris induction over convex sets, after comparing smooth and continuous singular cohomology; the outline follows that chapter.

statement: For every [real number](c:real-number) $\alpha$ and every [integer](c:integer) $N \ge 1$ there are integers $p$ and $q$ with $1 \le q \le N$ and $|q\alpha - p| \le 1/(N+1)$, so $p/q$ is a [rational approximation](c:rational-approximation) with $|\alpha - p/q| < 1/(qN)$.

hypotheses.text: The number $\alpha$ is a [real number](c:real-number).
The bound $N$ is an [integer](c:integer) with $N \ge 1$.

conclusion: Some integers $p, q$ with $1 \le q \le N$ satisfy $|q\alpha - p| \le 1/(N+1) < 1/N$.

formal.difference: The declaration works in the circle $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$ for any period $T > 0$, where $\|q\xi\|$ is the distance from $q\alpha$ to the nearest multiple of $T$. With $T = 1$ it is this statement.

proofs.name: Disjoint arcs on the circle
proofs.slogan: Place $N+1$ closed arcs of length $1/(N+1)$ at the points $j\alpha$ of the circle and show that two of them meet.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, in the circle $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$; the integer $p$ is the integer nearest to $q\alpha$.

roles.why: The number $\alpha$ gives the points $j\alpha$ on the circle.
$N \ge 1$ gives at least two arcs of total length 1, and it bounds $q = j - i$ by $N$.

steps.slogan: Center a closed arc of length $1/(N+1)$ at each point $j\alpha$ with $0 \le j \le N$.
steps.detail: Work in $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ with its [Haar measure](c:haar-measure) of total mass 1. The closed [ball](c:ball) $B_j$ of radius $\delta/2$ around $j\alpha$, with $\delta = 1/(N+1)$, has measure $\delta$, so the $N+1$ balls have total measure 1.

steps.slogan: Assume that the arcs are disjoint and show that they cover the circle.
steps.detail: Disjoint balls have a union of measure 1, the full measure. A [closed set](c:closed-set) of full measure is the whole circle, because its open complement has measure zero and every nonempty open set has positive measure.

steps.slogan: Contradict the [connectedness](c:connected-space) of the circle with this disjoint closed cover.
steps.detail: The circle would be a union of $N+1 \ge 2$ disjoint nonempty closed sets, so one ball and the union of the others would split it. This is impossible, so two balls $B_i$ and $B_j$ with $i < j$ meet.

steps.slogan: Bound $\|(j - i)\alpha\|$ by the triangle inequality through a common point.
steps.detail: For $x \in B_i \cap B_j$, $\|j\alpha - i\alpha\| \le \|j\alpha - x\| + \|x - i\alpha\| \le \delta$. So $q = j - i$ has $1 \le q \le N$ and $\|q\alpha\| \le 1/(N+1)$; take $p$ the integer nearest to $q\alpha$.

concepts.c:real-number: The real $\alpha$ gives the points $j\alpha$ of the circle.
concepts.c:integer: The integer $N$ counts the arcs and bounds the denominator $q$.
concepts.c:rational-approximation: The fraction $p/q$ is the approximation that the theorem produces.
concepts.c:haar-measure: The invariant measure gives every arc the same length.
concepts.c:ball: The arcs are closed balls of radius $1/(2N+2)$ on the circle.
concepts.c:closed-set: A closed set of full measure must be the whole circle.
concepts.c:connected-space: The connected circle cannot split into disjoint closed pieces.

source.note: mathlib applies NormedAddCommGroup.exists_norm_nsmul_le: disjoint closed balls would fill the circle by measure (measure_iUnion, addHaar_closedBall_center), against subsingleton_of_disjoint_isClosed_iUnion_eq_univ.

proofs.name: Pigeonhole on fractional parts
proofs.slogan: Sort the fractional parts of $0, \alpha, \dots, N\alpha$ and the number $1$ into $N+1$ short intervals and take two in one interval.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with integers $p$ and $q$ read off from the two chosen numbers.

roles.why: The number $\alpha$ supplies the fractional parts $\{j\alpha\}$.
$N \ge 1$ makes $1/(N+1) \le 1/2$ and bounds $q$ by $N$.

steps.slogan: List the $N+2$ numbers $0, \{\alpha\}, \dots, \{N\alpha\}, 1$ in $[0, 1]$.
steps.detail: Here $\{x\} = x - \lfloor x \rfloor$ with the [floor function](c:floor-function). Each listed number is $j\alpha - m$ with integers $0 \le j \le N$ and $m$; the number $1$ is $0 \cdot \alpha + 1$.

steps.slogan: Split $[0, 1]$ into $N+1$ closed intervals of length $1/(N+1)$.
steps.detail: The intervals $[k/(N+1), (k+1)/(N+1)]$ with $0 \le k \le N$ cover $[0, 1]$. There are $N+2$ numbers and $N+1$ intervals, so the pigeonhole principle puts two numbers into one interval.

steps.slogan: Show that the two numbers in one interval have different indices $j$.
steps.detail: Two numbers in one interval differ by at most $1/(N+1) \le 1/2$. The only pair with equal index is $0$ and $1$, which differ by 1, so the two indices differ.

steps.slogan: Subtract the two numbers to get $q$ and $p$.
steps.detail: If $j\alpha - m$ and $j'\alpha - m'$ with $j' < j$ lie in one interval, then $q = j - j'$ and $p = m - m'$ give $1 \le q \le N$ and $|q\alpha - p| \le 1/(N+1)$.

concepts.c:real-number: The real $\alpha$ supplies the fractional parts that are sorted.
concepts.c:integer: The integer $N$ fixes the number of intervals and points.
concepts.c:rational-approximation: The fraction $p/q$ is the approximation that the theorem produces.
concepts.c:floor-function: The floor function defines the fractional parts in $[0, 1)$.

source.note: Dirichlet's pigeonhole argument, as in G. H. Hardy and E. M. Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, chapter 11.

statement: Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded open set with $C^1$ [boundary](c:boundary) and outward unit [normal vector](c:normal-vector) $\nu$, and let $F$ be a $C^1$ [vector field](c:vector-field) on a neighborhood of $\overline{\Omega}$. Then $\int_\Omega \operatorname{div} F \, dV = \int_{\partial\Omega} F \cdot \nu \, dS$.

hypotheses.text: The set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is bounded and open, with $C^1$ [boundary](c:boundary) and outward unit [normal vector](c:normal-vector) $\nu$.
The [vector field](c:vector-field) $F$ is $C^1$ on a neighborhood of $\overline{\Omega}$.

conclusion: The volume integral of the [divergence](c:divergence) equals the flux, the [surface integral](c:surface-integral) $\int_{\partial\Omega} F \cdot \nu \, dS$.

formal.difference: The declaration treats only a rectangular box $[a, b]$, with the flux written as signed integrals over the faces. It assumes less regularity: continuity on the box, differentiability off a countable set inside it and an integrable divergence.

proofs.name: Boxes, then a partition of unity
proofs.slogan: Prove the formula on boxes from local linear estimates, then cut a general region into interior pieces and sheared boundary pieces.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Steps 1 and 2 are the box case that mathlib proves; steps 3 to 6 reduce a region with $C^1$ boundary to it.

roles.why: Boundedness gives a finite cover, and the $C^1$ boundary is locally a graph that the shear flattens.
The $C^1$ field is differentiable for the local estimates and keeps the sheared field of class $C^1$.

steps.slogan: Compare the face flux of $F$ on a small sub-box with its divergence term.
steps.detail: Let $J$ be a small, not too thin [box](c:box) that contains a point $x$. Differentiability at $x$ makes the difference of the integrals of $F_i$ over the two $i$-faces of $J$ equal to $\operatorname{vol}(J)\,\partial_i F_i(x)$ up to $\varepsilon \operatorname{vol}(J)$.

steps.slogan: Sum the local estimates over fine partitions to get the formula on a box.
steps.detail: The face flux is additive when a box is cut into sub-boxes. Summing step 1 over fine tagged partitions of a box $Q$ shows that $\int_Q \operatorname{div} F \, dV$ equals the outward flux through the faces of $Q$.

steps.slogan: Split $F$ by a [partition of unity](c:partition-of-unity) into fields with small supports.
steps.detail: Cover $\overline{\Omega}$ by finitely many small open boxes, each inside $\Omega$ or, after a rotation, meeting $\Omega$ in the part below a graph $x_n = \gamma(x')$ of a $C^1$ function. With a subordinate partition of unity $\{\varphi_k\}$, write $F = \sum_k \varphi_k F$; both sides are linear in $F$.

steps.slogan: Show that both sides vanish for a piece supported inside $\Omega$.
steps.detail: If $\varphi_k F$ has compact support inside a box $B \subset \Omega$, the box case on a closed box in $B$ around the support gives zero, because the field vanishes on its faces. The flux through $\partial\Omega$ is zero as well.

steps.slogan: Straighten a boundary piece by the shear $\Phi(x', t) = (x', \gamma(x') + t)$.
steps.detail: The shear has [Jacobian determinant](c:jacobian-determinant) 1 and maps $\{t < 0\}$ onto $\Omega$ near the piece. The field $G = (D\Phi)^{-1} F \circ \Phi$, with $G_n = (F_n - \sum_{i<n} \partial_i\gamma \, F_i) \circ \Phi$, has $\operatorname{div} G = (\operatorname{div} F) \circ \Phi$ by the chain rule.

steps.slogan: Apply the box case to $G$ and add up the pieces.
steps.detail: The box case on a half-box with top face $t = 0$ gives $\int_\Omega \operatorname{div} F = \int G_n(x', 0) \, dx'$, since $G$ vanishes on the other faces. Because $\nu \, dS = (-\nabla\gamma, 1) \, dx'$ on the graph, this is the flux of the piece; summing over $k$ gives the theorem.

concepts.c:boundary: The boundary is locally a graph, which the shear flattens.
concepts.c:normal-vector: The outward normal turns the flux into $(-\nabla\gamma, 1)\,dx'$ on a graph.
concepts.c:vector-field: The field is the object whose flux and divergence are compared.
concepts.c:divergence: The divergence is the sum of the partial derivatives estimated on boxes.
concepts.c:surface-integral: The flux is the surface integral of the normal component.
concepts.c:box: On boxes the flux splits into face integrals that add under subdivision.
concepts.c:partition-of-unity: It splits the field into pieces supported in single boxes.
concepts.c:jacobian-determinant: Determinant 1 makes the shear preserve volume and divergence integrals.

source.note: Steps 1 and 2 follow mathlib: BoxIntegral.hasIntegral_GP_divergence_of_forall_hasDerivWithinAt sums local estimates over tagged partitions, and the private lemmas integral_divergence_of_hasFDerivWithinAt_off_countable_aux1 and aux2 pass to the Bochner integral. mathlib has no general region, so steps 3 to 6 add the standard partition-of-unity reduction.

statement: Let $(f_k)_{k \ge 0}$ be a nonnegative [submartingale](c:martingale) with respect to a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_k)$ on a probability space. Then for every $\varepsilon \ge 0$ and $n \ge 0$, $\varepsilon \, P(\max_{k \le n} f_k \ge \varepsilon) \le E[f_n; \max_{k \le n} f_k \ge \varepsilon] \le E[f_n]$.

hypotheses.text: The process $(f_k)$ is a [submartingale](c:martingale): each $f_k$ is integrable and $\mathcal{F}_k$-measurable, and $E[f_{k+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_k] \ge f_k$.
Each $f_k$ is nonnegative.

conclusion: For $A = \{\max_{k \le n} f_k \ge \varepsilon\}$, $\varepsilon \, P(A) \le E[f_n \mathbf{1}_A] \le E[f_n]$.

formal.difference: The declaration works on any finite measure space, takes $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and states the first inequality in extended nonnegative reals. It omits the final bound by $E[f_n]$.

proofs.name: Stop at the first crossing
proofs.slogan: Stop the submartingale when it first reaches $\varepsilon$, and compare the stopped value with $f_n$ by optional stopping.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, including the trivial case $\varepsilon = 0$. Nonnegativity is used only for the last inequality.

roles.why: Adaptedness makes $\tau$ a stopping time, integrability makes all terms finite, and the submartingale property gives $E[f_\tau] \le E[f_n]$.
Nonnegativity of $f_n$ gives $E[f_n \mathbf{1}_A] \le E[f_n]$.

steps.slogan: Define the [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau$ as the first $k \le n$ with $f_k \ge \varepsilon$.
steps.detail: Set $\tau = \min\{k \le n : f_k \ge \varepsilon\}$, and $\tau = n$ if no such $k$ exists. The event $\{\tau = k\}$ depends only on $f_0, \dots, f_k$, so $\tau$ is a stopping time with $\tau \le n$.

steps.slogan: Bound the stopped value below by $\varepsilon$ on the event $A$.
steps.detail: On $A = \{\max_{k \le n} f_k \ge \varepsilon\}$ the time $\tau$ is a crossing time, so $f_\tau \ge \varepsilon$. Hence $\varepsilon P(A) \le E[f_\tau \mathbf{1}_A]$.

steps.slogan: Identify the stopped value with $f_n$ off the event $A$.
steps.detail: Off $A$ no $f_k$ with $k \le n$ reaches $\varepsilon$, so $\tau = n$ and $f_\tau = f_n$ there. Hence $E[f_\tau \mathbf{1}_{A^c}] = E[f_n \mathbf{1}_{A^c}]$.

steps.slogan: Compare $E[f_\tau]$ with $E[f_n]$ by optional stopping for bounded times.
steps.detail: For a submartingale and a stopping time $\tau \le n$, the [expected value](c:expected-value) satisfies $E[f_\tau] \le E[f_n]$. Indeed $E[f_n] - E[f_\tau] = \sum_{k<n} E[(f_{k+1} - f_k)\mathbf{1}_{\tau \le k}] \ge 0$, since $\{\tau \le k\} \in \mathcal{F}_k$.

steps.slogan: Subtract the common term $E[f_n \mathbf{1}_{A^c}]$ from both sides.
steps.detail: Steps 2 to 4 give $\varepsilon P(A) + E[f_n \mathbf{1}_{A^c}] \le E[f_\tau] \le E[f_n \mathbf{1}_A] + E[f_n \mathbf{1}_{A^c}]$, and the finite common term cancels. Finally $E[f_n \mathbf{1}_A] \le E[f_n]$ because $f_n \ge 0$.

concepts.c:martingale: The submartingale property makes stopping early lower the expectation.
concepts.c:filtration: The filtration decides which events are known at time $k$.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The first crossing time $\tau$ is the stopping time that splits $A$.
concepts.c:expected-value: The proof compares the expectations of $f_\tau$ and $f_n$.

source.note: mathlib stops at hittingBtwn f {y | eps <= y} 0 n, uses smul_le_stoppedValue_hittingBtwn on the event and Submartingale.expected_stoppedValue_mono for the comparison, then cancels the integral over the complement.

statement: Let $X$ be a real [normed space](c:normed-space) and $f\colon X \to (-\infty, +\infty]$ a proper function. Then $f = f^{**}$, where $f^*$ is the [convex conjugate](c:convex-conjugate) and $f^{**}(x) = \sup_{x^* \in X^*} (\langle x^*, x \rangle - f^*(x^*))$, if and only if $f$ is a [convex function](c:convex-function) and a [lower semicontinuous function](c:lower-semicontinuous-function).

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a real [normed space](c:normed-space) with [dual space](c:dual-space) $X^*$.
The function $f$ is proper: it never takes the value $-\infty$ and is not identically $+\infty$.

conclusion: $f = f^{**}$ holds exactly when $f$ is convex and lower semicontinuous.

proofs.name: Separation of the epigraph
proofs.slogan: Get $f^{**} \le f$ from the Fenchel-Young inequality, then separate a point below the closed convex epigraph to exclude $f^{**} < f$.
proofs.scope: Both directions. The hard direction splits into a non-vertical and a vertical separating hyperplane; the vertical case occurs only at points outside the domain of $f$.

roles.why: The dual $X^*$ defines $f^*$ and $f^{**}$, and Hahn-Banach separation works in $X \times \mathbb{R}$.
A point where $f$ is finite gives a non-vertical separation and so one affine minorant.

steps.slogan: Derive $f^{**} \le f$ from the Fenchel-Young inequality.
steps.detail: The definition of $f^*$ gives $\langle x^*, x \rangle - f^*(x^*) \le f(x)$ for all $x$ and $x^*$, so $f^{**} \le f$. The same computation shows that $f^{**}$ is the supremum of the continuous affine minorants $\langle x^*, \cdot \rangle - c$ of $f$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f^{**}$ is convex and lower semicontinuous.
steps.detail: A supremum of continuous affine functions has a closed convex epigraph, an intersection of closed half-spaces. So $f = f^{**}$ forces $f$ to be convex and lower semicontinuous.

steps.slogan: Find one continuous affine minorant $\ell_0$ of the convex lower semicontinuous $f$.
steps.detail: The epigraph of $f$ is a nonempty closed [convex set](c:convex-set) in $X \times \mathbb{R}$. For $f(x_1) < \infty$, Hahn-Banach separation of $(x_1, f(x_1) - 1)$ from it gives a [separating hyperplane](c:separating-hyperplane); it is not vertical because $(x_1, f(x_1))$ lies in the epigraph, so it is the graph of an affine minorant.

steps.slogan: Separate a point $(x_0, t)$ with $f^{**}(x_0) < t < f(x_0)$ from the epigraph.
steps.detail: Separation gives $x^* \in X^*$, $a \ge 0$ and $\gamma$ with $\langle x^*, x \rangle + a s > \gamma > \langle x^*, x_0 \rangle + a t$ on the epigraph. If $a > 0$, then $\ell = (\gamma - \langle x^*, \cdot \rangle)/a$ is a continuous affine minorant with $\ell(x_0) > t > f^{**}(x_0)$, against step 1.

steps.slogan: Tilt the minorant $\ell_0$ along the vertical hyperplane when $a = 0$.
steps.detail: If $a = 0$, then $\langle x^*, x \rangle > \gamma > \langle x^*, x_0 \rangle$ on the domain of $f$. The functions $\ell_0 + k(\gamma - \langle x^*, \cdot \rangle)$ with $k > 0$ are continuous affine minorants whose values at $x_0$ tend to $+\infty$, so $f^{**}(x_0) = +\infty$, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Combine the two inequalities and the two directions.
steps.detail: Steps 4 and 5 exclude $f^{**}(x_0) < f(x_0)$, and step 1 gives $f^{**} \le f$, so a convex lower semicontinuous $f$ equals $f^{**}$. Step 2 gives the converse.

concepts.c:normed-space: The normed space supplies continuous linear functionals for the affine minorants.
concepts.c:convex-conjugate: The conjugate $f^*$ defines the biconjugate $f^{**}$ that is compared with $f$.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity makes the epigraph a convex set that can be separated.
concepts.c:lower-semicontinuous-function: Lower semicontinuity makes the epigraph closed, which strict separation needs.
concepts.c:dual-space: Elements of $X^*$ are the slopes of the affine minorants.
concepts.c:convex-set: The epigraph is a closed convex set in the product space.
concepts.c:separating-hyperplane: A hyperplane between a point and the epigraph gives an affine minorant.

source.note: The separation proof of H. Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations, Springer 2011, theorem 1.11, arranged without the reduction to nonnegative functions.

statement: If a real function $f$ defined on an open [interval](c:interval) containing $a$ has a [local extremum](c:local-extremum) at $a$ and is differentiable at $a$, then its [derivative](c:derivative) vanishes there: $f'(a) = 0$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is defined on an open [interval](c:interval) that contains $a$.
The function $f$ has a [local extremum](c:local-extremum) at $a$.
The function $f$ is differentiable at $a$, with [derivative](c:derivative) $f'(a)$.

formal.difference: The declaration has no differentiability hypothesis, because mathlib sets $\operatorname{deriv} f\, a = 0$ when $f$ is not differentiable at $a$. For differentiable $f$ it is this statement.

proofs.name: Signs of one-sided difference quotients
proofs.slogan: At a local maximum the difference quotients are at most zero on the right and at least zero on the left, so their common limit is zero.
proofs.scope: A local maximum; a local minimum of $f$ is a local maximum of $-f$, whose derivative is $-f'(a)$.

roles.why: An open interval around $a$ allows increments $h$ of both signs.
The extremum fixes the sign of $f(a + h) - f(a)$ for small $h$.
Differentiability makes both one-sided limits of the quotient equal to $f'(a)$.

steps.slogan: Reduce a local minimum to a local maximum by passing to $-f$.
steps.detail: If $f$ has a local minimum at $a$, then $-f$ has a local maximum at $a$ and $(-f)'(a) = -f'(a)$. So it suffices to treat a local maximum.

steps.slogan: Get $f(a + h) - f(a) \le 0$ for all small $h$ of both signs.
steps.detail: At an interior local maximum there is $\delta > 0$ such that $(a - \delta, a + \delta)$ lies in the domain and $f(a + h) \le f(a)$ for $|h| < \delta$.

steps.slogan: Let $h \to 0^+$ in the [difference quotient](c:difference-quotient) to get $f'(a) \le 0$.
steps.detail: For $0 < h < \delta$, $(f(a + h) - f(a))/h \le 0$. The quotient tends to $f'(a)$ because $f$ is differentiable at $a$, so $f'(a) \le 0$.

steps.slogan: Let $h \to 0^-$ in the difference quotient to get $f'(a) \ge 0$.
steps.detail: For $-\delta < h < 0$ the numerator is at most zero and $h$ is negative, so the quotient is at least zero. Its limit $f'(a)$ is therefore at least zero.

steps.slogan: Combine the two inequalities into $f'(a) = 0$.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $0 \le f'(a) \le 0$, so $f'(a) = 0$ at a local maximum. By step 1 the same holds at a local minimum.

concepts.c:interval: The open interval lets $h$ approach zero from both sides.
concepts.c:local-extremum: The extremum gives the sign of the increments near the point.
concepts.c:derivative: The derivative is the common limit of the one-sided quotients.
concepts.c:critical-point: A zero derivative is the definition of a critical point.
concepts.c:difference-quotient: The quotients carry the sign information into the limit.

source.note: mathlib splits into IsLocalMin.deriv_eq_zero and IsLocalMax.deriv_eq_zero (the second through -f); IsLocalMaxOn.hasFDerivWithinAt_nonpos takes limits of c_n (f(a + d_n) - f(a)) <= 0 along every tangent direction, here both signs.

statement: Let $H$ be a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of a group $G$ and $k$ a commutative ring. For every $k[H]$-module $W$ and $k[G]$-module $V$, $\operatorname{Hom}_{k[G]}(\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W, V) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{k[H]}(W, \operatorname{Res}_H^G V)$ naturally, so [induction](c:induced-representation) is left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) to [restriction](c:restriction). For finite $G$ and $k = \mathbb{C}$, $\langle \operatorname{Ind}\chi, \psi \rangle_G = \langle \chi, \operatorname{Res}\psi \rangle_H$ for [characters](c:character-of-a-representation).

hypotheses.text: The group $H$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $G$, and $k$ is a commutative ring.
The modules $W$ over $k[H]$ and $V$ over $k[G]$ are [representations](c:group-representation) of $H$ and $G$ over $k$.
For the character identity, $G$ is finite and $k = \mathbb{C}$.

conclusion: Composition with $w \mapsto 1 \otimes w$ is a natural bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_{k[G]}(k[G] \otimes_{k[H]} W, V) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{k[H]}(W, V)$, and the character inner products agree.

proofs.name: Tensor-hom adjunction
proofs.slogan: Restrict a $G$-map from the induced module to $1 \otimes W$, and extend an $H$-map back by $g \otimes w \mapsto g\psi(w)$.
proofs.scope: The module statement for any group and commutative ring, then the character identity for finite groups over $\mathbb{C}$ by taking dimensions.

roles.why: The inclusion $k[H] \subseteq k[G]$ defines the tensor product and the restriction.
The module structures make $w \mapsto 1 \otimes w$ and the extended map linear.
For finite groups over $\mathbb{C}$, Hom dimensions are character inner products.

steps.slogan: Restrict a $G$-map $\varphi$ along the $H$-map $\iota(w) = 1 \otimes w$.
steps.detail: Here $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W = k[G] \otimes_{k[H]} W$, a [tensor product](c:tensor-product) over the [group ring](c:group-ring) $k[H]$. The map $\iota$ is $k[H]$-linear because $h \otimes w = 1 \otimes hw$, so $\Phi(\varphi) = \varphi \circ \iota$ is an $H$-map $W \to V$.

steps.slogan: Extend an $H$-map $\psi$ to the $G$-map $\Psi(\psi)(g \otimes w) = g\psi(w)$.
steps.detail: The map $(g, w) \mapsto g\psi(w)$ is balanced over $k[H]$, because $(gh, w)$ and $(g, hw)$ both go to $gh\psi(w) = g\psi(hw)$. The universal property of the tensor product makes $\Psi(\psi)$ a well-defined $k[G]$-linear map.

steps.slogan: Check that $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are mutually inverse and natural.
steps.detail: $\Phi(\Psi(\psi)) = \psi$, and $\Psi(\Phi(\varphi))(g \otimes w) = g\varphi(1 \otimes w) = \varphi(g \otimes w)$ on the spanning elements $g \otimes w$. Both maps commute with composition by module maps $W' \to W$ and $V \to V'$, so induction is left adjoint to restriction.

steps.slogan: Take complex dimensions of both Hom spaces to get the character identity.
steps.detail: For a finite group over $\mathbb{C}$, $\dim \operatorname{Hom}_G(U, V) = \langle \chi_U, \chi_V \rangle_G$ by Maschke's theorem, Schur's lemma and the orthogonality of characters. Step 3 gives equal dimensions, so the identity holds for characters, and by linearity for all class functions.

concepts.c:subgroup: The subgroup $H$ gives the smaller group ring and the restriction.
concepts.c:induced-representation: The induced module $k[G] \otimes_{k[H]} W$ is the left side of the bijection.
concepts.c:adjoint-functor: The natural bijection of Hom sets is exactly an adjunction.
concepts.c:restriction: Restriction views a representation of $G$ as one of $H$.
concepts.c:character-of-a-representation: Characters turn the Hom bijection into an equality of inner products.
concepts.c:group-representation: Representations are the modules on both sides of the bijection.
concepts.c:tensor-product: The tensor product over $k[H]$ builds the induced module.
concepts.c:group-ring: Modules over group rings are the representations in this proof.

source.note: The standard tensor-hom proof; for the character form see J.-P. Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups, section 7.2.

statement: Let $1 \le p < n$ and $p^* = np/(n - p)$. There is a constant $C = C(n, p)$ such that $\|u\|_{L^{p^*}(\mathbb{R}^n)} \le C \, \|Du\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)}$ for every $C^1$ function $u\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ with [compact support](c:compact-support), where both sides are [Lebesgue space](c:lp-space) norms.

hypotheses.text: The exponents satisfy $1 \le p < n$ and $p^* = np/(n - p)$.
The function $u\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is $C^1$ with [compact support](c:compact-support).

conclusion: $\|u\|_{L^{p^*}} \le C(n, p) \, \|Du\|_{L^p}$ with a constant independent of $u$, so the [Sobolev](c:sobolev-space) seminorm controls the $L^{p^*}$ norm.

formal.difference: The declaration is the case $p = 1$, $p^* = n/(n - 1)$, on any finite-dimensional real normed space with an additive Haar measure and with values in a Banach space. The general $p$ is the separate declaration eLpNorm_le_eLpNorm_fderiv_of_eq.

proofs.name: Grid lines and Hölder
proofs.slogan: Bound $|u|$ by line integrals of $|Du|$, integrate one variable at a time with Hölder, then raise $|u|$ to a power for $p > 1$.
proofs.scope: Steps 1 to 3 prove the case $p = 1$; steps 4 and 5 deduce $1 < p < n$ from it. For $u = 0$ both sides vanish.

roles.why: The bound $p < n$ makes $\gamma$ finite and $p^*$ the exponent that balances the powers of $|u|$.
Compact support and $C^1$ regularity justify the line integrals and keep $|u|^\gamma$ of class $C^1$.

steps.slogan: Bound $|u(x)|$ by the integral of $|Du|$ along each coordinate line.
steps.detail: Compact support and the fundamental theorem of calculus give $u(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x_i} \partial_i u(x_1, \dots, y_i, \dots, x_n) \, dy_i$. Hence $|u(x)| \le \int_{\mathbb{R}} |Du| \, dy_i$ for each $i$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the $n$ line bounds and take the power $1/(n - 1)$.
steps.detail: This gives $|u(x)|^{n/(n-1)} \le \prod_{i=1}^n (\int_{\mathbb{R}} |Du| \, dy_i)^{1/(n-1)}$. The $i$-th factor does not depend on $x_i$.

steps.slogan: Integrate in $x_1, \dots, x_n$ in turn, with Hölder on $n - 1$ factors each time.
steps.detail: At each integration one factor is constant in the variable, and the generalized Hölder inequality with $n - 1$ exponents equal to $n - 1$ handles the others. After $n$ steps $\int |u|^{n/(n-1)} \le (\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |Du|)^{n/(n-1)}$, the case $p = 1$.

steps.slogan: Apply the case $p = 1$ to $v = |u|^\gamma$ with $\gamma = p(n - 1)/(n - p)$.
steps.detail: For $1 < p < n$, $\gamma > 1$, so $v$ is $C^1$ with compact support and $|Dv| \le \gamma |u|^{\gamma - 1} |Du|$. Step 3 gives $(\int |u|^{\gamma n/(n-1)})^{(n-1)/n} \le \gamma \int |u|^{\gamma - 1} |Du|$.

steps.slogan: Split the right side by Hölder and divide by the common factor.
steps.detail: Hölder with exponents $p/(p - 1)$ and $p$ bounds the right side by $\gamma (\int |u|^{(\gamma - 1)p/(p - 1)})^{(p-1)/p} \|Du\|_p$. The choice of $\gamma$ makes both powers of $|u|$ equal to $p^*$, and division gives $\|u\|_{p^*} \le \gamma \|Du\|_p$; for $p = 1$ step 3 is the claim.

concepts.c:compact-support: Compact support lets each line integral start from zero.
concepts.c:lp-space: The inequality compares norms in two Lebesgue spaces $L^{p^*}$ and $L^p$.
concepts.c:sobolev-space: The gradient norm $\|Du\|_{L^p}$ is the Sobolev seminorm being controlled.

source.note: mathlib proves the case p = 1 by the grid-lines lemma lintegral_prod_lintegral_pow_le, an induction over the coordinates with Hölder (ENNReal.lintegral_mul_prod_norm_pow_le); eLpNorm_le_eLpNorm_fderiv_of_eq_inner does steps 4 and 5 with |u|^gamma.

statement: For every element $a$ of a complex unital [Banach algebra](c:banach-algebra) $A$, the limit $\lim_{n \to \infty} \|a^n\|^{1/n}$ exists and equals the [spectral radius](c:spectral-radius) $r(a) = \sup\{|\lambda| : \lambda \in \sigma(a)\}$, where $\sigma(a)$ is the [spectrum](c:spectrum-of-an-operator) of $a$.

hypotheses.text: The algebra $A$ is a unital [Banach algebra](c:banach-algebra) with $\|1\| = 1$.
The scalars of $A$ are the complex numbers.

formal.difference: The declaration states the limit in the extended nonnegative reals. It does not need $\|1\| = 1$.

proofs.name: Spectral mapping below, resolvent series above
proofs.slogan: Bound $r(a)$ by every $\|a^n\|^{1/n}$ through the spectrum of $a^n$, and bound the limit superior by the radius of the resolvent power series.
proofs.scope: The whole formula: the lower bound holds for each $n \ge 1$, the upper bound for the limit superior. If $r(a) = 0$, the disc of step 3 is the whole plane.

roles.why: Completeness makes Neumann series converge and the invertible elements an open set.
Complex scalars give holomorphy and the Cauchy integral formula.

steps.slogan: Show that every spectral value $\mu$ of an element $b$ has $|\mu| \le \|b\|$.
steps.detail: If $|\mu| > \|b\|$, the Neumann [geometric series](c:geometric-series) $\sum_k b^k/\mu^{k+1}$ converges in the complete algebra to an inverse of $\mu - b$. So $\mu \notin \sigma(b)$.

steps.slogan: Map spectral values of $a$ to spectral values of $a^n$ and bound them.
steps.detail: For $\lambda \in \sigma(a)$, $a^n - \lambda^n = (a - \lambda)q(a)$ with commuting factors, so $a^n - \lambda^n$ is not invertible and $\lambda^n \in \sigma(a^n)$. Step 1 gives $|\lambda|^n \le \|a^n\|$, so $r(a) \le \|a^n\|^{1/n}$ for all $n$ and $r(a) \le \liminf \|a^n\|^{1/n}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $z \mapsto (1 - za)^{-1}$ is holomorphic on the disc $|z| < 1/r(a)$.
steps.detail: For $z \ne 0$, $1 - za = z(1/z - a)$ is invertible unless $1/z \in \sigma(a)$, which needs $|z| \ge 1/r(a)$. Inversion is holomorphic on the open group of invertible elements, so the map is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) on that disc.

steps.slogan: Expand the resolvent map in its power series $\sum_n z^n a^n$ on the whole disc.
steps.detail: Near $0$ the map equals the Neumann series $\sum_n z^n a^n$. By the Cauchy integral formula, a holomorphic Banach-valued function equals its Taylor series on every disc where it is holomorphic, so this [power series](c:power-series) has [radius of convergence](c:radius-of-convergence) at least $1/r(a)$.

steps.slogan: Read off $\limsup \|a^n\|^{1/n} \le r(a)$ from the Cauchy-Hadamard formula and conclude.
steps.detail: The Cauchy-Hadamard theorem gives the radius $1/\limsup \|a^n\|^{1/n}$, so $\limsup \|a^n\|^{1/n} \le r(a)$. With step 2, $\limsup \le r(a) \le \liminf$, so the limit exists and equals $r(a)$.

concepts.c:banach-algebra: Completeness and the submultiplicative norm drive both bounds.
concepts.c:spectral-radius: The spectral radius is the claimed limit of $\|a^n\|^{1/n}$.
concepts.c:spectrum-of-an-operator: Spectral values of powers give the lower bound.
concepts.c:geometric-series: The Neumann series inverts elements close to a scalar.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy of the resolvent controls the series on a large disc.
concepts.c:radius-of-convergence: The radius links the growth of the norms to the spectrum.
concepts.c:power-series: The series $\sum z^n a^n$ carries the norms $\|a^n\|$ as coefficients.

source.note: mathlib combines spectralRadius_le_liminf_pow_nnnorm_pow_one_div (spectral mapping and norm_le_norm_mul_of_mem) with limsup_pow_nnnorm_pow_one_div_le_spectralRadius, which reads the radius of the series of z -> (1 - z a)^(-1) from differentiableOn_inverse_one_sub_smul and DifferentiableOn.hasFPowerSeriesOnBall.

statement: Let $M$ be a [closed](c:closed-manifold) oriented [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of even dimension $2n$, and let $\Omega$ be the [curvature form](c:curvature-form) of its Levi-Civita connection. Then the [Euler characteristic](c:euler-characteristic) of $M$ is $\chi(M) = \int_M \operatorname{Pf}(\Omega / 2\pi)$, the integral of the [Pfaffian](c:pfaffian) of the curvature.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ is [closed](c:closed-manifold): compact and without boundary.
The manifold $M$ is oriented and carries a [Riemannian](c:riemannian-manifold) metric.
The dimension of $M$ is even, $\dim M = 2n$.

proofs.name: Chern's transgression on the sphere bundle
proofs.slogan: Write the Pfaffian as an exact form on the unit sphere bundle, integrate it over the section given by a vector field, and count indices.
proofs.scope: An outline of Chern's intrinsic proof; the transgression formula of step 2 and the index limit of step 4 rest on the cited paper. Odd dimensions are not treated.

roles.why: Without boundary, Stokes' theorem leaves only the small spheres, and Poincaré-Hopf applies.
The metric gives the curvature and the unit sphere bundle; the orientation makes the Pfaffian a global form.
The Pfaffian exists for skew matrices of even size $2n$.

steps.slogan: Form the Pfaffian of the curvature matrix in oriented orthonormal frames.
steps.detail: In an oriented orthonormal frame the curvature form is a skew $2n \times 2n$ matrix $\Omega$ of 2-forms. Its Pfaffian is invariant under $SO(2n)$, so $\operatorname{Pf}(\Omega/2\pi)$ is a global $2n$-form on $M$.

steps.slogan: Write the pulled-back Pfaffian as an exact form on the unit sphere bundle.
steps.detail: On the unit [sphere bundle](c:sphere-bundle) $\pi\colon SM \to M$, Chern builds a $(2n-1)$-form $\Pi$ from the connection and curvature forms whose exterior derivative is $\pi^* \operatorname{Pf}(\Omega/2\pi)$. This [transgression](c:transgression-of-differential-forms) is the main computation of the paper.

steps.slogan: Pull back $\Pi$ by the unit field of a vector field with isolated zeros.
steps.detail: Take a [vector field](c:vector-field) $X$ with isolated zeros $p_1, \dots, p_k$; away from them $s = X/|X|$ is a section of $SM$. Stokes' theorem turns $\int_{M \setminus \bigcup_i B_\varepsilon(p_i)} \operatorname{Pf}(\Omega/2\pi)$ into a sum of integrals of $s^*\Pi$ over the small spheres $\partial B_\varepsilon(p_i)$.

steps.slogan: Let the spheres shrink and identify each sphere integral with an index of $X$.
steps.detail: On each fiber, $\Pi$ restricts to the normalized volume form of $S^{2n-1}$, and its other terms vanish as $\varepsilon \to 0$. So the $i$-th sphere integral tends to the index of $X$ at $p_i$, and $\int_M \operatorname{Pf}(\Omega/2\pi) = \sum_i \operatorname{ind}_{p_i} X$.

steps.slogan: Identify the index sum with $\chi(M)$ by the Poincaré-Hopf theorem.
steps.detail: The Poincaré-Hopf theorem says that the indices of a vector field with isolated zeros on a closed manifold add up to the Euler characteristic. Hence $\chi(M) = \int_M \operatorname{Pf}(\Omega/2\pi)$.

concepts.c:closed-manifold: A closed manifold has no boundary terms and a finite index sum.
concepts.c:riemannian-manifold: The metric determines the curvature form that is integrated.
concepts.c:curvature-form: The curvature matrix of 2-forms is the input of the Pfaffian.
concepts.c:euler-characteristic: The Euler characteristic is the topological side of the formula.
concepts.c:pfaffian: The Pfaffian turns the curvature matrix into a top-degree form.
concepts.c:sphere-bundle: On the sphere bundle the Pfaffian becomes exact.
concepts.c:transgression-of-differential-forms: Transgression supplies the primitive form whose boundary integrals count indices.
concepts.c:vector-field: Its zeros localize the integral and their indices give the count.

source.ref: S.-S. Chern, A simple intrinsic proof of the Gauss-Bonnet formula for closed Riemannian manifolds, Annals of Mathematics 45 (1944), no. 4, 747-752
source.note: Chern's intrinsic proof: transgression of the Pfaffian on the unit sphere bundle and the index limit at the zeros of a vector field, closed by the Poincaré-Hopf theorem.
